title: AI Use at U.S. Businesses (Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users)
key_claim: BTOS data for December 2025 to May 2026 show overall AI usage hovering between 17% and 20% (national rate 19.8% on 3 May 2026); 37% of firms with at least 250 employees used AI versus less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees, and use increased among firms with at least 20 employees but not significantly among firms with fewer than 20.
frame_summary: Argues that AI use among U.S. businesses is rising but remains modest and sharply skewed by firm size, with large firms adopting fastest and the smallest firms barely moving.
verbatim_quote: overall AI usage hovered between 17% and 20%; 37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI in their business operations; the AI use rates in the Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) sectors were both higher than the national rate (19.8%); Less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI.
notes: Primary firm-level adoption anchor; the firm-size divergence is the operational concentration signal.

title: Monitoring AI Adoption in the US Economy (FEDS Notes)
date_evidence: meta-citation_publication_date: 04-03-2026 (i.e. 2026-04-03); URL slug monitoring-ai-adoption-in-the-u-s-economy-20260403.html; author Jeffrey S. Allen
key_claim: Reconciling three surveys, the note reports a BTOS firm-weighted AI adoption rate of about 18% for December 2025 against an employment-weighted firm adoption rate of around 78% and an LLM rate of about 54%, showing that adoption is concentrated among the large firms that employ most workers.
frame_summary: Argues that headline AI-adoption numbers diverge widely by method, and that employment-weighting reveals adoption concentrated among the large firms that employ most workers.
verbatim_quote: Table 1 reports the BTOS December 2025 firm-weighted AI adoption estimate at 18 percent; the SBU estimates an employment-weighted firm AI adoption rate of around 78 percent and an LLM adoption rate of about 54 percent.
notes: Employment-weighted vs firm-weighted gap is the clearest quantitative read on concentration among large employers.

publisher: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
title: Measuring AI Adoption among Firms: How You Ask Matters (On the Economy)
date_evidence: visible byline 'June 01, 2026' by Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin, David Deming ; canonical .../on-the-economy/2026/jun/measuring-ai-adoption-firms-how-you-ask-matters
key_claim: Argues the low firm-level AI-adoption numbers are mostly a survey-design artifact: worker surveys put on-the-job AI use at roughly 35% to 40% while the old BTOS question put firm use at just 5% to 7%; revising the question to 'any business function' in November 2025 nearly doubled measured adoption to about 17%, and an EU extrapolation implies a U.S. any-purpose rate near 34%.
frame_summary: Argues that the apparent gap between high worker AI use and low firm AI adoption is mostly a survey-design artifact, not evidence of slow firm-level diffusion.
verbatim_quote: Worker surveys suggest that somewhere around 35% to 40% of workers use AI on the job, while the main U.S. firm survey put AI adoption among businesses at just 5% to 7%. ... the measured adoption rate almost doubled to 17%. ... we arrive at an estimated 34%, a figure that would place the U.S. among the highest-adoption countries in Europe.
notes: Counter-argument anchor: adoption breadth is real once measured; the signal must rest on value not headcount.

title: The 2026 AI Index Report, Economy chapter
date_evidence: Multiple sources confirm the 2026 AI Index Report was published on April 13, 2026; report page header '04 Economy | The 2026 AI Index Report'.
key_claim: Organizational AI adoption rose to 88% of surveyed organizations in 2025 and generative AI reached 53% population adoption in three years (faster than the PC or internet), yet AI agent deployment was in the single digits across nearly all business functions and productivity gains were largest only in structured, measurable work.
frame_summary: Argues that AI capability, investment and organizational adoption are all rising fast, but that deployment of autonomous agents and realized economic impact remain early and uneven.
verbatim_quote: Organizational AI adoption continued to rise in 2025, up to 88% of surveyed organizations, though AI agent use remains early. Generative AI is now used in at least one business function at 70% of organizations. Generative AI reached 53% adoption in three years, faster than the personal computer or the internet.
notes: Consensus-framing source and partial counter-argument (fast diffusion); agents single-digit corroborates the scaling gap.

title: 2026 AI Performance Study (press release: three-quarters of AI's economic gains captured by 20% of companies)
key_claim: A survey of 1,217 senior executives across 25 sectors finds nearly three-quarters (74%) of AI's economic value is captured by just one-fifth (20%) of organisations, with the majority of businesses still stuck in pilot mode; AI leaders are far more likely to redesign workflows, reinvent the business model and increase decisions made without human intervention.
frame_summary: Argues that a small minority of companies is capturing most of AI's financial value by using it to reinvent business models, while the majority remain stuck in pilots.
verbatim_quote: nearly three-quarters (74%) of AI's economic value is captured by just one-fifth (20%) of organisations, revealing a stark and widening divide between a small group of AI leaders and the majority of businesses still stuck in pilot mode.
notes: Headline value-concentration anchor for the signal.

title: AI growth acceleration versus distributional fairness
date_evidence: visible article date 'May 5, 2026'; background guide distributed ahead of the Forum for Cooperation on AI dialogue on March 31, 2026
key_claim: Argues that AI adoption, first concentrated in information-intensive and professional-services tasks, is now diffusing into physically constrained sectors, but that even at high stated adoption realized employment and productivity impacts remain limited and that AI-investing firms seek more skilled staff, alter hierarchies and contribute to rising industry concentration.
frame_summary: Argues that AI's growth benefits and its risks are distributed unevenly, with adoption and gains concentrating among larger, more capable firms and pressure falling on entry-level pathways.
notes: Mechanism source: links the value gap to rising industry concentration and entry-level risk; adds US/UK/EU breadth.

title: 12 Graphs That Explain the State of AI in 2026
date_evidence: 'The article was published on April 13, 2026' (IEEE Spectrum, by Matthew S. Smith), covering Stanford's 2026 AI Index
key_claim: In its survey of the 2026 AI Index, IEEE Spectrum reports that 2025 set a record for AI investment with over US $581 billion spent while AI's overall impact on employment remains mixed, with entry-level roles in exposed professions reduced even as mid-career and senior roles held steady.
frame_summary: Argues, in surveying the 2026 AI Index, that AI investment and capability are surging while AI's measured impact on jobs and the broader economy remains mixed and uncertain.
verbatim_quote: 2025 set a new record for AI investment with over US $581 billion spent. That's more than double the $253 billion spent in 2024.
notes: Independent journalism corroboration of the investment surge that is not yet translating into broad value.
